object_types.name: Account
object_types.definition: The customer entity in the system; everything hangs off it. Identified by account number, six digits, sequential, never reused.

source_references.excerpt: An account. Every account has an account number. That's what everything hangs off.
Yes. Six digits, sequential, never reused.

object_types.name: AccountNumber
object_types.definition: The six-digit sequential unique identifier of an account, never reused.

source_references.excerpt: Six digits, sequential, never reused.

object_types.name: Subscription
object_types.definition: The agreement that an account pays a specific amount on a cycle for a product; identified by subscription ID.

source_references.excerpt: A subscription is the agreement that this account pays us this amount on this cycle for this thing. It's got a subscription ID.

object_types.name: SubscriptionId
object_types.definition: Unique generated identifier for a subscription, prefixed with SUB.

source_references.excerpt: Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.

object_types.name: Product
object_types.definition: A product offered by the company, identified by a product code. Fixed set today: CORE, ANALYTICS, CONNECT (fourth in discovery).

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: ProductCode
object_types.definition: The code identifying a product.

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: PricePlan
object_types.definition: The billing artefact that generates the invoice line -- specifies what the customer pays and how often. Identified by plan code. Also referred to as 'plan' by Priya, distinct from feature bundle.

source_references.excerpt: The price plan. It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

object_types.name: PlanCode
object_types.definition: The code identifying a price plan, e.g. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490.

source_references.excerpt: CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

object_types.name: FeatureBundle
object_types.definition: What the customer gets -- the feature bundle (seats, API, SSO), the thing on the pricing page. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. Identified by name.

source_references.excerpt: When I say plan I mean what the customer gets. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. It's the feature bundle -- how many seats, whether they get the API, whether they get SSO.
Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. There's no code, which annoys me.

object_types.name: FeatureBundleName
object_types.definition: The unique name identifying a feature bundle, e.g. Starter, Professional, Enterprise.

source_references.excerpt: Yes. There's exactly one Professional.

object_types.name: StartDate
object_types.definition: The date a subscription begins; mandatory.

source_references.excerpt: Start date is always there. You can't create a subscription without one, the form won't submit.

object_types.name: EndDate
object_types.definition: The date a subscription ends; optional, present for fixed-term subscriptions or after cancellation of annual subscriptions (set to paid-through date).

source_references.excerpt: An open-ended subscription has no end date. Most of them are open-ended -- they run until cancelled. A fixed-term one has an end date agreed up front, that's usually an enterprise deal.

object_types.name: BillingPeriod
object_types.definition: The cycle on which a subscription is billed: monthly or annual.

source_references.excerpt: Monthly or annual.
Never neither. Every subscription has exactly one billing period.

object_types.name: SubscriptionStatus
object_types.definition: The status of a subscription: trialing, active, past due, or cancelled.

source_references.excerpt: Trialing, active, past due, cancelled.
Exactly one, yes.

object_types.name: PausedFlag
object_types.definition: A separate boolean flag indicating a subscription is paused, distinct from and overlapping confusingly with status.

source_references.excerpt: Paused isn't a status, it's a flag.
It behaves like a status but it isn't one, it's a separate boolean, which is exactly why it causes bugs.

object_types.name: MRR
object_types.definition: Monthly recurring revenue; derived from the price plan price normalised to a month, not stored anywhere in the source system.

source_references.excerpt: Every subscription has an MRR. Monthly recurring revenue.
It's worked out. It's the plan price normalised to a month. An annual plan at 490 is an MRR of 40.83.

object_types.name: PlanChange
object_types.definition: A record of a change to a subscription's price plan, with its own identity (change ID), effective date, requester, and the new price plan. Belongs to exactly one subscription.

source_references.excerpt: A change is a record. We don't overwrite the plan on the subscription, we write a plan change with an effective date, and the subscription's current plan is derived from the change history.
It's got a change ID.

object_types.name: ChangeId
object_types.definition: Unique identifier of a plan change.

source_references.excerpt: It's got a change ID.

object_types.name: EffectiveDate
object_types.definition: The date on which a plan change takes effect.

source_references.excerpt: Someone can make a change on the third that takes effect on the first of next month.

object_types.name: Requester
object_types.definition: The person who requested a plan change.

source_references.excerpt: It records the subscription, the new price plan, the effective date, and who requested it.

ambiguities.description: Three different concepts are all called 'plan' in the business: the billing price plan (Priya's usage), the feature bundle (Tom's usage), and the sales-negotiated deal (mentioned but out of scope). The model resolves PricePlan and FeatureBundle as separate entities, but the sales 'deal' concept is not modeled at all -- is it needed, and if so what identifies it?

source_references.excerpt: So we've got two things both called plan. ... We've got two things both called plan, and the sales team calls a third thing a plan, which is the deal they negotiated, which frequently matches neither.

ambiguities.description: Whether an account that closes and later returns as 'the same company' should be treated as a new Account (per current rule) or historically linked is a known point of tension between Product and Finance. No linking mechanism is modeled; is this acceptable long-term or should a company-level entity be introduced?

source_references.excerpt: If an account closes and the same company comes back, they get a new number and we treat them as a new customer for reporting. ... Which drives me mad, incidentally, because from a product perspective it's the same company and we lose the history.

ambiguities.description: The 'one active subscription per account per product' constraint is enforced at the database level, but the transcript doesn't clarify how 'active' interacts with the four-value SubscriptionStatus and the separate PausedFlag -- does 'active' here mean status='active' specifically, or any non-terminal status (e.g. trialing, past due)? This affects how the uniqueness constraint should be scoped/filtered.

source_references.excerpt: So it's one active subscription per account per product.
It behaves like a status but it isn't one, it's a separate boolean, which is exactly why it causes bugs. If you ask the system for active subscriptions you get paused ones too.

ambiguities.description: PausedFlag's mandatory/optional status and its interaction rules with SubscriptionStatus (e.g., can a cancelled subscription be paused?) are not specified. Is PausedFlag mandatory on every Subscription, and are there exclusions with certain statuses?

source_references.excerpt: There's also paused. ... It behaves like a status but it isn't one, it's a separate boolean, which is exactly why it causes bugs.

ambiguities.description: The commercial policy for mid-term cancellation of annual subscriptions (run to term vs prorated refund vs credit) is explicitly undecided and parked by the facilitator. Only the current system behavior (end date set to paid-through date, no refund mechanism) is captured; the business rule is not finalized.

source_references.excerpt: What happens commercially when an annual subscription is cancelled mid-term -- run to term, prorated refund, or credit -- is undecided. The model will capture the system behaviour, which is that cancellation sets an end date and access runs to it, and it will not invent a refund concept that doesn't exist.

ambiguities.description: The relationship between PlanChange's recorded new PricePlan and the Subscription's current (denormalised) PricePlan is a derived/maintained relationship (change process maintains current plan), and if they disagree, change history wins and current plan is treated as a bug. This suggests the 'current PricePlan' role on Subscription is itself derived from PlanChange history rather than independently asserted -- should it be modeled as a stored (denormalized, maintained) attribute or purely derived? The transcript indicates both views were expressed before resolving to 'stored but derived/maintained'.

source_references.excerpt: One correction. You said a subscription belongs to one price plan. It doesn't, really -- that's what the plan changes are for. ... No, Sam, it does have a current plan field. The changes are the history, but there's a denormalised current plan on the record.
Correct. And if those two ever disagree, the change history wins and the current plan is the bug.

ambiguities.description: MRR is explicitly derived (plan price normalised to a month) and not stored; however the exact formula/rounding (e.g. how 490 annual becomes 40.83 monthly) is not fully specified for other billing periods or edge cases (e.g. mid-cycle proration), leaving the derivation rule only partially defined.

source_references.excerpt: It's worked out. It's the plan price normalised to a month. An annual plan at 490 is an MRR of 40.83.
